result: Shamsi called these the most successful builds yet. She picked D as best (C was close, but has no footer) and B as worst. Three of four used the sort bar; two put the category list in a modal (B, D) and one in a popover (C), and Shamsi liked C's popover. What is left is proximity: controls too close to each other and to the text above, loose spacing in B, and an information icon too small to notice.

A.notes: Accordions for the category list and the explanation; believed a popover or modal is not allowed without JavaScript.

B.notes: Modals with an inline script; an icon-only information button.

C.notes: Popover with its own inline script; no footer; dropped the figure placeholders on all sections.

D.notes: Modals; did not render its pages. Without JavaScript the explanation is out of reach.

patterns: Sort bar in three of four (none in round 8), after the routing row and the rule for choosing.
Category list: a modal in B and D, a popover in C, an accordion in A (none in round 8).
Refresh with its icon on the updated line in all four.
The design system has no script for opening a popover, so C and B wrote their own and A thought it could not use one.
Proximity was the remaining weak spot: the Categories button sat against the sort bar, and the sort bar against the text above.
Predictions: 1 right (three of four used the sort bar). 2 right (three of four used a popover or modal). 3 right (Refresh with its icon on the updated line in all four).
findings: Two groups of controls for one list need a row with one group at each end, close to the list and apart from the text above it.
An information button needs a visible label; an icon alone is missed.
A status tag in a card belongs in its top corner, so it does not push the card's content down out of line with its neighbours.
next: Document the toolbar row, the labelled information button and the tag in the card's corner; then decide whether to run one more round or move the work to PR 9.
